title: Two Crabs
description: A still life makes crabs the central subject, contrasting their forms and red shells against a green ground. This is an appearance in art history, not a claim about religious symbolism.

title: Crustaceans
description: More than a hundred carefully observed crabs fill the work, showing the animal as a subject of sustained artistic attention.

title: Box in the Form of a Crab
description: The crab’s body becomes the shape of a functional container: an example of the animal translated into an everyday luxury object.

title: Rookwood crab-decorated dish
description: The Met connects the scattered crab motifs on this dish with compositional patterns in books by Hokusai and his pupils, documenting the motif’s movement between artistic traditions.

title: Battle of the Monkey & the Crab
description: A conflict between a monkey and a crab develops into a revenge tale. The crab and its allies drive the story; this is Japanese folklore, not automatically a Shinto religious narrative.

title: Karkinos and the Hydra
description: The crab intervenes against Heracles and is rewarded by Hera with a place among the stars. Its importance is the link between a heroic episode and Cancer.

title: The Crane and the Crab
description: A crab sees through a crane’s false promise of rescue. The animal’s decisive response makes deceit and discernment the center of a religious teaching story.

title: The Time Machine
description: In the far future, the traveler encounters monstrous crab-like creatures on a desolate shore. Their appearance helps convey an Earth transformed beyond human civilization.

title: The Young Crab & His Mother
description: A mother criticizes her child’s sideways walk, but cannot demonstrate the straight walking she demands. Crab movement becomes a lesson about teaching by example.

title: The Crab and the Fox
description: A crab leaves the seashore and is caught by a fox. The short narrative uses displacement from a familiar habitat to make its moral point.
